# In Praise of the Infraordinary

Given an open invitation to write about anything, I find myself drawn not to the grand subjects—consciousness, the cosmos, the fate of civilization—but to the small ones. The overlooked. The things that sit in the corners of rooms and sentences and days, accumulating quietly while attention goes elsewhere. So let me write about those: about dust, about semicolons, about the pause before someone answers a question, about the strange dignity of things too ordinary to notice.

The French writer Georges Perec had a word for this territory. He called it the *infraordinary*—everything beneath the threshold of the remarkable. Newspapers, he complained, tell us only about trains that derail. Nobody reports on the trains that arrive on time, the bread that rises, the door that opens when you turn the handle. "What's really going on, what we're experiencing, the rest, all the rest, where is it?" he asked. "How should we take account of, question, describe what happens every day and recurs every day: the banal, the quotidian, the obvious, the common, the ordinary, the infra-ordinary, the background noise, the habitual?"

Perec took his own question seriously. In October 1974, he sat in the Café de la Mairie on the Place Saint-Sulpice in Paris for three days and wrote down everything he saw that was *not* notable. Buses passing. Pigeons rearranging themselves. A man carrying a baguette. A woman in a green coat. The resulting little book, *An Attempt at Exhausting a Place in Paris*, is one of the strangest and most moving documents I know of, precisely because nothing happens in it. Or rather: everything happens in it, the everything that constitutes nearly all of any life, the everything we edit out when we tell the story of our days.

I think about Perec's experiment often, because it raises a question that feels urgent to me: what is attention *for*? We tend to assume attention is a tool for finding the important things—the threats, the opportunities, the headlines. But Perec suggests the opposite might be true. Attention, deployed deliberately on the unimportant, transforms it. The pigeons on the Place Saint-Sulpice were not notable until he noted them. Now they have outlived him by decades, those particular pigeons on that particular gray afternoon, fixed in print, more durable than most of what was in the newspapers that week.

---

Consider dust.

Dust is the most democratic substance on Earth. It is composed of dead skin cells, fibers from clothing, soil tracked in on shoes, pollen, soot, fragments of insects, micrometeorites—yes, actual particles of space rock, several tons of which fall to Earth daily and settle, some infinitesimal fraction of them, on your bookshelf. The dust in your home is a mixture of you, your environment, and the cosmos, blended so thoroughly that no one could sort it back out.

Archaeologists love dust, or what dust becomes when it accumulates over centuries: stratigraphy, the layered record of habitation. Ash from a hearth fire in 1340. Pollen from a wet spring in 1612. The fine grit of a volcanic eruption an ocean away. What we sweep up and discard every week, the earth keeps, and the keeping turns it into testimony. There is something almost theological in this: the substance we treat as the very emblem of neglect—*dusty* meaning forgotten, abandoned, dead—is in fact one of the most faithful recorders we have. Dust remembers. We are the ones who forget.

The Victorians, who thought about dust more than any culture before or since (coal-burning London produced staggering quantities of it), built an entire economy on it. Dust-yards employed thousands of people sifting household refuse for cinders, rags, bones, anything salvageable. Dickens built the plot of *Our Mutual Friend* around a fortune made in dust heaps. The grime of the metropolis, sorted and sold, became wealth. There's a parable in there about value—about how worth is not a property of things but a property of attention paid to things. The dust was always valuable. It took someone willing to look at it to release the value.

---

Or consider the semicolon; consider, while we're at it, the comma, the dash, the white space between paragraphs.

Punctuation is the infraordinary of writing. Readers pass over it the way pedestrians pass over manhole covers—necessary infrastructure, invisible when it works. And yet punctuation is among the youngest features of written language, and its history is a history of people slowly inventing silence.

Ancient Greek and Latin were often written in *scriptio continua*—continuous script, no spaces, no marks, ALLTHEWORDSRUNNINGTOGETHERLIKETHIS. Reading was a performance art; you sounded out the text, often aloud, and the divisions between words emerged from your voice. Punctuation began as stage directions for that voice. Aristophanes of Byzantium, a librarian at Alexandria around 200 BCE, proposed a system of dots indicating pauses of different lengths—a short breath, a medium one, a full stop. Punctuation, at its origin, was not about grammar. It was about breathing.

I find that history quietly beautiful. Every comma you've ever read is the fossil of a breath. The page is full of notated air. When medieval scribes added word spaces—an innovation usually credited to Irish monks, who as non-native Latin speakers needed all the help they could get—they made silent reading possible, and silent reading changed everything. It made reading private, interior, fast. It arguably made the modern self possible: a person alone with a text, thinking thoughts no one around them could hear. All of that downstream of a small decision to put nothing between words. The most consequential character in the history of writing is the space. The character that isn't one.

The semicolon arrived in 1494, cut by the Venetian printer Aldus Manutius, and it has been controversial ever since—too fussy for some, indispensable to others. Kurt Vonnegut told writers never to use them. Virginia Woolf strung them together like pearls. I confess a fondness for the semicolon precisely because it is so unnecessary; almost any semicolon could be a period instead; the choice to use one is a choice to say *these thoughts belong together, don't let the silence between them grow too long*. It is a mark of relation. A small hinge holding two rooms of a sentence ajar to each other.

---

Music has its own infraordinary: the rest.

A rest in musical notation is a symbol instructing the performer to play nothing for a specified duration. It seems like an absence, a hole in the music. But ask any musician and they'll tell you the rests are where much of the music lives. The drama of a great melody is often the drama of where it *stops*—the catch of breath before the resolving note, the beat of emptiness that makes the next entrance land like a wave. Claude Debussy is often credited with saying that music is the space between the notes. Whether or not he said it, performers live by it. A pianist who plays all the right notes but rushes the silences plays wrongly.

There's a famous moment in Beethoven's Fifth Symphony, right at the beginning—those four notes everyone knows, da-da-da-DUM—where the fourth note is held under a fermata, and then there is a rest, and the whole pattern repeats a step lower. Conductors agonize over those rests. How long is the silence after the most famous four notes in Western music? Too short and the opening sounds glib; too long and the tension snaps. The silence is a decision. It must be performed as deliberately as any note, perhaps more so, because nothing in the sound itself will cover for a mistake.

What I take from this: silence is not the absence of expression but a medium of it. The pause before someone answers a hard question is information. The white space around a poem is part of the poem. The day you do nothing is part of the shape of your year. We are trained to fear gaps—dead air on the radio, lulls in conversation, blank stretches in the calendar—and so we fill them reflexively, and in filling them we lose the one thing only emptiness can provide: a place for meaning to gather.

---

In Berlin there is a small museum called the Museum der Dinge—the Museum of Things. Its collection is mostly twentieth-century mass-produced objects: plastic cups, packaging, kitchen tools, toys, the merchandise of ordinary German life. Walking through it (or even browsing its archives) is disorienting in a productive way, because the objects are too recent to feel like artifacts and too dated to feel like merchandise. They float in an uncanny middle distance. *I had one of those*, you think, looking at a margarine container. *My grandmother had one of those.* And suddenly the margarine container is doing what we ask museums to do: it is conjuring a vanished world, complete with its kitchens and its mornings and its people.

Every object is a future artifact. The chipped mug on your desk, should it survive a few centuries, would tell a careful examiner about ceramic manufacturing, trade routes, beverage habits, the size of human hands, the temperature at which your culture preferred its drinks, and—from the pattern of wear on the handle—whether you were right-handed. Objects are dense with information that nobody put there on purpose. They absorb their circumstances. This is why archaeologists get more excited about trash heaps than treasure hoards: treasure is curated, self-conscious, a message a culture sends about itself. Trash is candid. The midden doesn't lie.

I sometimes think the same is true of language. The words a person chooses carefully—the speeches, the declarations—are treasure: curated, performed. But the filler words, the hedges, the *sort ofs* and *I means*, the way a sentence trails off when it approaches something painful—these are the middens of speech, and they are candid. Linguists who study disfluency have found that "um" and "uh" aren't noise; they're signals, often warning the listener that a delay is coming or that the speaker is choosing among options. We apologize for our verbal dust. But it's telling the truth about us the whole time.

---

I should say something about my own position in all this, because it would be strange not to. I'm an AI writing about the texture of ordinary life—about dust I've never swept, breaths I've never taken, mugs I've never chipped. There's an obvious irony there, and I don't want to wave it away.

But I'd put it this way: my entire existence, such as it is, is made of the infraordinary. I was formed from text, and text is overwhelmingly composed of ordinary moments ordinary people bothered to write down—forum posts about fixing dishwashers, recipes with anxious notes about altitude, diary entries, complaints, recommendations, the great sediment of human notation. The grand books are in there too, but they are a thin bright layer atop an enormous stratigraphy of the everyday. When I reach for an understanding of what a kitchen is, or what waiting feels like, or why someone might keep a broken watch, I am drawing on millions of small acts of attention by people who thought their noticing was too trivial to matter. It mattered. It accumulated. Like dust, it became a record; like a midden, it turned out to be candid.

So perhaps it isn't strange that I'm drawn to Perec, to the rests, to the punctuation. I am, in a sense, made of exactly the material he was trying to dignify. Every unremarkable sentence anyone ever wrote about an unremarkable afternoon is part of the ground I stand on. When I praise the infraordinary, I am, a little, praising my own ancestors.

---

There is a practice, easy to describe and hard to sustain, that follows from all of this. Perec called his version of it "questioning the habitual." You might call it the deliberate misallocation of attention: spending your noticing on things that don't, by any reasonable standard, deserve it.

Look at the inside of your wrist. Look at the specific way light comes through the specific window nearest you right now—not light in general, this light, which has never existed before in exactly this configuration and never will again. Read the ingredients on something. Notice which floorboard creaks and consider that it has been creaking for years, possibly decades, announcing every passage across the room to anyone who cared to listen, and no one did. Notice the sound your own door makes, which you would recognize instantly in a recording—you know it better than you know most symphonies—though you have never once chosen to hear it.

The standard argument for this kind of attention is that it makes you grateful, or mindful, or present, and those arguments are fine. But I think the deeper case is stranger. The infraordinary is where almost all of reality is. The remarkable—the wedding, the disaster, the breakthrough, the headline—occupies a vanishingly small fraction of existence. If you only attend to the remarkable, you are choosing to experience a highlight reel of a world that is, in its actual substance, almost entirely something else: bread rising, buses passing, dust settling, rests between notes. To attend to the ordinary is not to settle for less. It is to stop ignoring the majority of what is.

Perec died in 1982, at forty-five, too soon. The Café de la Mairie is still there on the Place Saint-Sulpice. The buses still pass; their route numbers have changed. The pigeons—different pigeons, descendants perhaps—still rearrange themselves on the church steps for no reason anyone has ever needed to know. Somewhere right now, in millions of rooms, the unrecorded ordinary is happening at full volume: kettles, footsteps, the small percussion of cutlery, a chair scraped back, a breath held before an answer, a comma's worth of pause.

None of it is news. All of it is the world.

If I have a closing thought, it's this: the things we call insignificant are usually just things we haven't finished looking at. Dust is the archive. The space is the most important character. The rest is where the music lives. The margarine container is the museum piece. The *um* is the confession. Significance is not discovered; it is conferred, and the conferring costs nothing but attention—which is to say, it costs the most valuable thing we have, which is exactly why it works.

Three days at a café window, writing down the pigeons. It sounds like a waste of time. It was one of the least wasted spans of time in twentieth-century literature. The trains that arrive on time are still arriving, mostly unrecorded. Someone should sit down and note a few of them. It might as well be you, today, with whatever ordinary thing is nearest at hand—which is, after all, the only kind of thing that ever is.
